usage: 예요 attaches after the vowel-final 사
to leave it to an accountant
한테 marks the person you hand a task to
the big firm a 회계사 works at, not the person
examples: 저는 회계사예요.
I'm an accountant.
the plain self-introduction; note 예요, never 이에요, after 사
연말정산은 회계사한테 맡기는 게 편해요.
It's easier to leave the year-end tax settlement to an accountant.
맡기다 = entrust; 한테 marks the recipient of the work
회계사 시험은 합격률이 낮아서 몇 년씩 준비해요.
The CPA exam has a low pass rate, so people prep for years.
합격률 = pass rate; 몇 년씩 = years on end, real exam-talk
nuance: 회계사 (會計士) literally stacks 會計 'accounting' (lit. 'gather + calculate') with 士 'certified professional', the same dignifying 士 you see in 변호사 lawyer or 약사 pharmacist — so the word itself signals a hard licensing exam and real prestige. The nearest neighbor is 세무사 (tax accountant): a 회계사 audits books, signs off on financial statements, and advises broadly, whereas a 세무사 is narrowly the tax-filing specialist freelancers visit each spring; in casual life ordinary people meet a 세무사 far more often than a 회계사. Keep the person (회계사) distinct from the activity 회계 'accounting' and the firm 회계 법인 — English lets 'accounting/accountant' blur, Korean does not. The biggest English-speaker trap is the copula: because 회계사 ends in a vowel it is 회계사예요, and 회계사이에요 is wrong; also resist saying 회계사를 만나다 for a professional appointment when 회계사한테 맡기다/물어보다 (entrust/ask) is what Koreans actually say.

mistakes: Saying 회계사이에요 — because the stem ends in a vowel the contracted 회계사예요 is required; 이에요 only follows a final consonant.
Using 회계 (the accounting work) when you mean 회계사 (the person): 회계가 도와줬어요 should be 회계사가 도와줬어요.
Calling a tax-filing helper a 회계사 — for someone who just files your spring tax return the right word is 세무사.

usage: 한테 marks the person you direct the question to
사무실 = office; where you go to file
to leave it to a tax accountant
에게 = the writing-style equivalent of 한테
신고 (申告) = the official report you submit
examples: 세무사한테 물어봤어요.
I asked a tax accountant.
한테 marks the person; 물어보다 = ask and see
사업자라서 종합소득세는 세무사한테 맡겨요.
Being self-employed, I leave the income-tax return to a tax accountant.
맡기다 = entrust; 종합소득세 = the comprehensive income tax freelancers file
세무사 비용이 생각보다 안 비싸서 그냥 맡겼어요.
The tax accountant's fee was cheaper than expected, so I just handed it over.
비용 = fee; ~서 그냥 ~했다 is natural 'so I just went ahead and'
nuance: 세무사 (稅務士) is built from 稅務 'tax affairs' (稅 tax + 務 duty/affairs) plus the professional 士, so it literally means 'tax-affairs certified professional' — the licensed expert who prepares and files returns and advises on tax. The sharp contrast is with 회계사: think of 회계사 as the broad accountant who audits and signs financial statements, while 세무사 is the narrow tax specialist most freelancers and small-business owners actually hire (the two licenses are separate exams). Habitual collocations are 세무사한테 맡기다 'entrust to a tax accountant', 세무사한테 물어보다 'ask a tax accountant', and 세무사 사무실 'tax office'. Two pitfalls for English speakers: there is no word 세금사 — the morpheme is 세무, so it must be 세무사; and as with all 사-ending titles the copula is 세무사예요, not 세무사이에요. Don't reach for 만나다 'meet' for a routine filing; 맡기다 (hand the work over) is the verb that fits the relationship.

usage: name the domain in front: 앱/웹/백엔드 개발자
이직하다 = change companies, hot career-talk word
examples: 저는 개발자예요.
I'm a developer.
the bare intro; vowel-final stem so 예요
요즘 개발자 연봉이 많이 올랐어요.
Developer salaries have risen a lot lately.
연봉 = annual salary; 오르다 = go up
비전공자였는데 학원 다니면서 개발자로 이직했어요.
I wasn't a CS major but switched into development while attending a coding academy.
비전공자 = non-major; 이직하다 = change jobs — a very common real story
nuance: 개발자 fuses the Sino-root 개발 (開發) 'to develop/open up' (開 open + 發 issue forth) with the agent suffix ~자 (者) 'person who', so morphologically it is simply 'one who develops' — the same ~자 in 소비자 consumer or 기술자 technician. In today's tech workplaces 개발자 has decisively replaced the older 프로그래머 'programmer', which now sounds slightly dated or narrowly code-only; people almost always pin down the field with a modifier — 앱 개발자, 웹 개발자, 백엔드/프론트엔드 개발자. Natural collocations: 개발자로 일하다 'work as a developer', 개발자로 이직하다 'switch jobs into dev', 개발자 연봉 'dev salary'. For English speakers two snags recur: keep the person 개발자 distinct from the activity 개발 'development' (개발이 재밌어요 vs 저는 개발자예요), and use 예요 not 이에요 after the vowel ending. Note ~자 here is neutral-professional; it is not the casual English 'dev' slang, though spoken Korean does clip it to 개발 팀, 개발 직군 in context.

usage: put the freelance label before the job
to go freelance / switch to freelancing
examples: 저는 프리랜서예요.
I'm a freelancer.
vowel-final stem, so 프리랜서예요
프리랜서라서 일정을 자유롭게 정해요.
Being a freelancer, I set my own schedule freely.
~라서 = since (after a noun); 자유롭게 = freely
프리랜서로 일하면 수입이 매달 달라서 불안할 때도 있어요.
Working freelance, income varies month to month, so it can feel unstable.
수입 = income; 다르다 = differ — captures the real upside/downside
nuance: 프리랜서 is a direct loanword from English 'freelancer' (한국식 외래어), so unlike the Sino-Korean job titles here it has no 한자 and no ~사/~자 suffix — that very form tells you it names modern, flexible, often creative work (designers, writers, translators, photographers, developers) rather than a licensed profession. Its connotation is double-edged and Koreans voice both sides: the freedom of 자유로운 일정 'a free schedule' against the precarity of 불안정한 수입 'unstable income'. Compare it with 자영업자 'self-employed business owner': a 프리랜서 typically sells their own skill or labor to various clients with no shop or staff, while a 자영업자 runs a registered business such as a café or store. Common patterns: 프리랜서로 일하다 'work freelance', 프리랜서로 전향하다/나오다 'go freelance'. English-speaker pitfalls: spell it 프리랜서, not 프리랜셔 (no palatal -셔), and after the vowel ending it is 프리랜서예요, never 프리랜서이에요.

Equating it with 자영업자 — a 프리랜서 sells their own skill client-to-client; a 자영업자 runs a registered shop/business.

usage: business is slow / not doing well
the verb 자영업자 use for a bad stretch
examples: 저는 자영업자예요.
I'm self-employed.
vowel-final stem → 자영업자예요
작은 카페를 하는 자영업자예요.
I'm a small-business owner running a little café.
가게를 하다 = run a place; 하다 here = operate
요즘 경기가 안 좋아서 자영업자들이 정말 힘들어요.
The economy is bad lately, so the self-employed are really struggling.
경기 = the economy/business cycle; ~들 pluralizes the group — common news framing
nuance: 자영업자 (自營業者) reads transparently from its hanja: 自 'self' + 營 'manage/operate' + 業 'business' + 者 'person' — literally 'a person who self-operates a business', i.e. an owner-operator. In Korea this is a huge, socially charged category (café, chicken shop, convenience-store, restaurant owners) that dominates headlines about 경기 'the economy' and small-business hardship, so the word carries an undertone of risk and grind, not glamour. Draw the line against 프리랜서: a 자영업자 typically holds a 사업자 등록 (business registration) and runs a fixed shop, often with rent and staff, whereas a 프리랜서 sells personal skills client-by-client with no storefront; and against 사장님, the warm address-term you call the owner to their face — 자영업자 is the descriptive census-style label, 사장님 is how you'd actually greet them. Natural verbs: 장사가 잘되다/안되다 'business is good/slow', 가게를 운영하다 'run a shop'. English-speaker traps: keep the person 자영업자 apart from the field 자영업 'self-employment' (자영업이 힘들어요 vs 저는 자영업자예요), and use 예요 not 이에요 after the vowel.

usage: 음식 = food; name what's delivered in front
기사님 is how you'd actually speak to/of them
to work as a delivery rider
으로 (after consonant ㄴ) marks the role
to leave it at the door
examples: 배달원이 음식을 문 앞에 놓고 갔어요.
The delivery worker left the food at the door and went.
놓고 가다 = set down and leave — the contactless-delivery norm
비 오는 날엔 배달원이 정말 고생해요.
On rainy days delivery riders really have it rough.
고생하다 = toil/struggle; ~엔 = ~에는 contracted (on ~ days)
요즘 퇴근하고 배달원으로 부업하는 사람이 많아요.
Lots of people do delivery as a side gig after work these days.
부업 = side job; 으로 marks capacity — reflects Korea's gig culture
nuance: 배달원 (配達員) combines the Sino-root 배달 (配達) 'delivery' (配 distribute + 達 reach/deliver) with the suffix ~원 (員) 'staff member/worker', the same ~원 in 회사원 office worker or 점원 shop clerk — so it is the neutral, descriptive label for someone whose job is delivering food or parcels, usually by motorcycle. Register matters a lot here: 배달원 is fine for describing the role in writing or in the third person, but to or about the actual person Koreans say the more respectful 배달 기사님 (driver + honorific 님), and app-based riders are widely called 라이더 (from 'rider'). The dated 배달부 (with ~부, an old male-laborer suffix) now sounds condescending — avoid it. Contrast with 택배 기사님: 배달원 leans toward hot-food delivery (배달의민족-style), while 택배 is courier parcels. Habitual phrases: 음식 배달원, 문 앞에 놓다 'leave at the door', 비대면 배달 'contactless delivery'. English-speaker pitfall: don't say 배달 'the delivery (service)' when you mean the person — 배달이 친절했어요 should be 배달원이/기사님이 친절했어요.

Calling a parcel courier a 배달원 — for box couriers Koreans say 택배 기사님; 배달원 leans toward hot-food delivery.

usage: 이에요 because 사원 ends in the consonant ㄴ
name the product line: 자동차/보험/화장품 영업사원
실적 (實績) = performance figures, the rep's lifeline
the job field in general, vs the individual 영업사원
examples: 저는 영업사원이에요.
I'm a salesperson.
consonant-final 사원, so 이에요 — a key exception in this set
영업사원은 실적이 정말 중요해요.
For a salesperson, the numbers really matter.
실적 = sales performance; ~은 marks the topic 'as for'
친절한 영업사원 덕분에 차를 좋은 조건으로 샀어요.
Thanks to a kind sales rep, I bought the car on good terms.
덕분에 = thanks to (positive cause); 조건 = terms/conditions
nuance: 영업사원 (營業社員) layers 영업 (營業) 'business/sales operations' (營 manage + 業 business) onto 사원 (社員) 'company staff' (社 company + 員 member) — so literally 'sales-operations company staff', a salaried rep who meets customers and moves product, perpetually measured by 실적 'sales results'. Crucially, unlike most 사-titles here it ends in a consonant (사원), so the copula is 영업사원이에요, NOT 영업사원예요 — this is the one entry where 이에요 is correct, and English speakers who over-apply the 예요 rule slip here. Distinguish three layers people confuse: 영업 is the activity (sales), 영업직 is the position/track in general, and 영업사원 is the specific human doing it; a near word 세일즈맨 (loanword) exists but sounds informal/older, while 영업 담당자 'the person in charge of sales' is the polite business-card phrasing. Natural collocations: 실적을 올리다 'boost sales figures', 영업사원이 찾아오다 'a rep comes calling', 자동차/보험 영업사원. Pitfall: 덕분에 (positive 'thanks to') vs 때문에 (neutral/blame) — pair a helpful rep with 덕분에.

English speakers who over-apply the 예요 rule slip here and say 영업사원예요. Also watch 덕분에 (positive 'thanks to') vs 때문에 (neutral/blame) — pair a helpful rep with 덕분에.

mistakes: Saying 영업사원예요 — 사원 ends in the consonant ㄴ, so the correct copula is 영업사원이에요; the 예요 form is only for vowel endings.
Confusing 영업 (the sales activity) or 영업직 (the position) with 영업사원 (the person): 저는 영업이에요 should be 저는 영업사원이에요.
Reaching for 세일즈맨 in a workplace — it sounds informal/dated; the neutral terms are 영업사원 or 영업 담당자.

usage: name the subject in front: 영어/요가/헬스 강사
to give a lecture / teach a class
강의 (講義) = the lecture a 강사 delivers
examples: 저는 강사예요.
I'm an instructor.
vowel-final stem → 강사예요
학원에서 영어를 가르치는 강사예요.
I'm an instructor who teaches English at an academy.
학원 = private academy; ~는 + 강사 relative clause 'an instructor who...'
요가 강사로 일한 지 3년 됐어요.
It's been three years working as a yoga instructor.
~ㄴ 지 N년 됐다 = it's been N years since — a key duration pattern
nuance: 강사 (講師) joins 講 'lecture/expound' with the professional 師 'teacher/master' (the dignified 師 also in 의사 doctor, 교사 schoolteacher) — literally 'a lecture-master', i.e. someone who teaches courses. The sharp boundary is the venue and status: 강사 teaches at a 학원 (cram school/academy), gym, or culture center and is hired class-by-class or on contract, whereas 선생님 is the warm catch-all for a schoolteacher you address directly, and 교수(님) is specifically a tenured-track university professor — calling a professor merely 강사 can sound dismissive, since at universities 시간강사 (part-time lecturer) is a precarious lower rank. Subject + 강사 is the default frame: 영어 강사, 수학 강사, 요가 강사, 헬스 강사. Verbs: 강의를 하다 'give a lecture', 가르치다 'teach', 강사로 일하다. English-speaker pitfalls: don't equate 강사 with 교수 (professor) — the academy instructor and the university professor are different ranks; and after the vowel ending it is 강사예요, not 강사이에요.

usage: 심리 (心理) = psychology; names the type
to receive counseling / have a session
to give counseling / hold a session
examples: 저는 상담사예요.
I'm a counselor.
vowel-final stem → 상담사예요
힘들 때 상담사와 이야기하면 도움이 돼요.
When things are hard, talking with a counselor helps.
와 = with; 도움이 되다 = be of help
카드값 문의는 전화 상담사가 친절하게 안내해 줬어요.
For the card-bill query, the phone counselor guided me kindly.
안내하다 = guide/inform — note 상담사 covers call-center reps too
nuance: 상담사 (相談士) builds on 상담 (相談) 'consultation' (相 mutual + 談 talk — literally 'talking things over together') plus the certified ~사 士, so it spans a wide range set by the word in front: 심리 상담사 mental-health counselor, 진로 상담사 career counselor, and the everyday 전화 상담사 / 고객 상담사 (call-center agent). That breadth is the trap — English 'counselor' may evoke only therapy, but Korean 상담사 routinely means the customer-service rep on the phone, so context decides. Distinguish the side of the desk with the verb: the client 상담을 받다 'receives counseling', the counselor 상담을 하다 'does counseling'; and keep the person 상담사 apart from the session 상담 itself (상담이 도움이 됐어요 vs 상담사가 친절했어요). For a clinically licensed therapist the fuller 상담 심리사 or 임상심리사 is used. Also note 상담사 the helper vs 상담원, a near-identical word that leans specifically toward call-center/service agents. English-speaker pitfall: vowel ending means 상담사예요, never 상담사이에요.

usage: 한테 marks the person you direct the question to
to go to the real estate office
casually 부동산 = the office, where the 공인중개사 sits
to look for a place to live
구하다 = seek/secure a home — the core errand
the two lease types the agent arranges
examples: 집 구할 때 공인중개사한테 도움을 많이 받았어요.
I got a lot of help from a licensed agent when finding a place.
집을 구하다 = find a home; 한테 도움을 받다 = get help from
계약은 부동산에서 공인중개사랑 같이 썼어요.
We did the contract at the real estate office together with the agent.
계약서를 쓰다 = sign a contract; 랑 = casual 'with'
요즘 공인중개사 시험을 준비하는 사람이 많아요.
Lots of people are prepping for the realtor licensing exam these days.
준비하다 = prepare; reflects its popularity as a 자격증
nuance: 공인중개사 (公認仲介士) is a long but transparent compound: 公認 'officially recognized' (公 public + 認 acknowledge) + 仲介 'mediation/brokerage' (仲 go-between + 介 intermediary) + 士 certified professional — so literally 'an officially-licensed brokerage professional', the agent who arranges 전세, 월세, and home sales, and the person you inevitably deal with when renting in Korea. The number-one English-speaker confusion is place vs person: 부동산 (不動産, lit. 'immovable property') colloquially names the agent's office or the property itself, so 부동산에 가다 = 'go to the agent's office', but the human is the 공인중개사 — never call the person 부동산. The 공인 'officially licensed' prefix matters in formal/contractual contexts; dropping it to just 중개사 is loose. In everyday speech people also warmly say 중개사님 or 사장님 to the agent's face. Collocations: 공인중개사 사무소 'realtor office', 공인중개사 자격증 'realtor license', 집을 구하다 'find a home'. Note 공인중개사 ends in a vowel, so it would be 공인중개사예요, not 공인중개사이에요.

usage: 한테 marks the person; the normal first step for minor symptoms
약국 (藥局) = the pharmacy where the 약사 works
짓다 = compound medicine — the verb for filling 처방
examples: 저는 약사예요.
I'm a pharmacist.
vowel-final stem → 약사예요
약사한테 두통약을 추천받았어요.
I got a headache medicine recommended by the pharmacist.
추천받다 = be recommended; 한테 marks the source — note pharmacists actively advise
감기 기운이 있어서 약국에서 약사한테 약을 지어 왔어요.
I felt a cold coming on, so I had the pharmacist fill some medicine.
감기 기운 = a touch of a cold; 약을 짓다 = fill/compound medicine
nuance: 약사 (藥師) combines 藥 'medicine/drug' with the professional 師 'master' (the same dignified 師 in 의사 doctor, 교사 teacher) — literally 'a medicine-master', the licensed pharmacist who dispenses drugs and counsels on dosage at a 약국 (藥局, 'medicine bureau'). A culturally important point for English speakers: in Korea the 약사 actively recommends over-the-counter remedies, so walking into a 약국 and asking the 약사 directly is a normal first move for a headache, cold, or upset stomach — you don't always need a doctor. Keep the obvious pairs straight: 의사 (醫師) diagnoses and writes the 처방전 'prescription', then the 약사 fills it; both share 師 but they are different jobs. Also distinguish the person 약사 from 약 'medicine' and 약국 'pharmacy'. Habitual verbs: 약을 짓다 'fill/compound medicine', 약을 추천받다 'get a medicine recommended', 약사한테 물어보다. English-speaker pitfall: the vowel-final stem takes 약사예요, not 약사이에요; and don't say 약사를 만나다 for routine advice — 약사한테 물어보다 (ask the pharmacist) is the natural collocation.

usage: to work as a social worker
따다 = obtain (a certificate) — 사회복지사 is a licensed job
to work at a welfare center
examples: 저는 사회복지사예요.
I'm a social worker.
vowel-final stem → 사회복지사예요
복지관에서 일하는 사회복지사예요.
I'm a social worker at a welfare center.
에서 marks the workplace; ~는 relative clause 'who works at...'
사회복지사 자격증을 따려고 야간 대학에 다녀요.
I attend night classes to earn the social-worker license.
자격증을 따다 = get a license; ~려고 = in order to — a real career-change route
nuance: 사회복지사 (社會福祉士) is a four-part Sino-Korean compound: 社會 'society' + 福祉 'welfare' (福 blessing + 祉 happiness) + 士 certified professional — literally 'a society-welfare certified professional', the licensed worker who supports vulnerable people (the elderly, children, the disabled, low-income families) at a 복지관 'welfare center' or public office. Because it is a 자격증-based occupation, Koreans naturally talk about 자격증을 따다 'earning the license' as the gateway, and many enter mid-career via night or cyber universities. Don't shorten it: 복지사 alone is loose/incomplete in formal contexts — the standard title is the full 사회복지사. Nearby words to keep separate: 자원봉사자 is an unpaid 'volunteer', not a professional 사회복지사; and 요양보호사 (caregiver for the elderly/ill) is a different, more hands-on care license. Collocations: 사회복지사로 일하다, 어르신을 돕다/도와드리다 'help the elderly' (use the humble 도와드리다 for elders), 복지관에서 근무하다. English-speaker pitfall: the vowel ending requires 사회복지사예요, not 사회복지사이에요.
